# OSS Scanner build for cryptsetup.
#
# Two builds are produced from the same checkout in /src:
#   /src/build       gcc, debugoptimized, -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Mirrors a distribution build;
#                    use it to run the upstream test suite (meson test -C /src/build).
#                    Tools: /src/build/src/{cryptsetup,veritysetup,integritysetup}
#   /src/build-asan  clang, AddressSanitizer + UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, libFuzzer targets enabled.
#                    Use it to confirm memory-safety findings and to run the fuzzers:
#                      /src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/crypt2_load_fuzz
#                      /src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/crypt2_load_ondisk_fuzz
#                      /src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/crypt_load_misc_fuzz
#                    Tools: /src/build-asan/src/{cryptsetup,veritysetup,integritysetup}
#
FROM ubuntu:26.04

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive \
    LANG=C.UTF-8

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      ca-certificates git build-essential clang libclang-rt-dev lld llvm meson ninja-build pkg-config \
      autoconf automake autopoint libtool gettext \
      libssl-dev libdevmapper-dev libpopt-dev uuid-dev libjson-c-dev libssh-dev \
      libblkid-dev libkeyutils-dev \
      sharutils dmsetup jq xxd expect keyutils netcat-openbsd passwd \
      openssh-client sshpass xz-utils tar file e2fsprogs util-linux kmod gdb \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# scanner contract: the checkout lives inside the image, at /src
COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src

# 1) Reference build (distribution-like: OpenSSL backend incl. Argon2, debug info, frame pointers).
RUN meson setup /src/build /src \
      --buildtype=debugoptimized \
      -Dc_args="-g -fno-omit-frame-pointer" \
      -Dasciidoc=disabled \
      -Dnls=false \
      -Dcrypto-backend=openssl \
      -Dargon-implementation=none \
    && meson compile -C /src/build

# 2) Sanitizer + fuzzer build (same OpenSSL backend incl. Argon2).
#    b_lundef=false is required when linking with -fsanitize=*.
RUN CC=clang CXX=clang++ meson setup /src/build-asan /src \
      --buildtype=debug \
      -Db_sanitize=address,undefined \
      -Db_lundef=false \
      -Dc_args="-g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined" \
      -Dcpp_args="-g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined" \
      -Dfuzz-targets=true \
      -Dcrypto-backend=openssl \
      -Dargon-implementation=none \
      -Dasciidoc=disabled \
      -Dnls=false \
    && meson compile -C /src/build-asan

# Sanitizer defaults for anyone running the ASan binaries in this image.
ENV ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1:symbolize=1 \
    UBSAN_OPTIONS=print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1

# Smoke tests that need neither root device-mapper nor a kernel module: crypto vectors, wipe,
# utility units and exported-symbol checks. Failures are reported but never abort the build.
# The full suite (meson test -C /src/build) needs root, device-mapper and loop devices; it can be
# run inside the scanner's privileged VM.
RUN cd /src/build && (meson test --no-rebuild --print-errorlogs --timeout-multiplier 3 \
        vectors-test unit-wipe-test unit-utils-crypt-test run-all-symbols \
      || echo "WARNING: cryptsetup smoke tests reported failures")

# Quick sanity check that the sanitized fuzzers start (no crash on the empty input).
RUN for f in crypt2_load_fuzz crypt2_load_ondisk_fuzz crypt_load_misc_fuzz; do \
      /src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/$f -runs=1 >/dev/null 2>&1 \
        || echo "WARNING: fuzzer $f failed its smoke run"; \
    done

FROM node:lts-trixie

WORKDIR /src
COPY . .

# Generic tools
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates make git wget tar curl && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Pnpm
RUN npm install -g pnpm@11.1.2

# Go
RUN wget https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.2.linux-amd64.tar.gz
RUN rm -rf /usr/local/go && tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.2.linux-amd64.tar.gz
RUN rm -rf go1.27.2.linux-amd64.tar.gz
ENV PATH=$PATH:/usr/local/go/bin
RUN go version

# Deps
RUN make deps

# Test to ensure build is working
RUN make webui
RUN make test
RUN make clean-webui

FROM node:24-bookworm AS node
FROM rust:1-bookworm

# The scanner uses Linux x86-64. On ARM hosts, build with
# DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM=linux/amd64 (also for tools/check).
COPY --from=node /usr/local/ /usr/local/
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive \
    HUSKY=0 \
    ELECTRON_SKIP_BINARY_DOWNLOAD=1 \
    PLAYWRIGHT_SKIP_BROWSER_DOWNLOAD=1 \
    CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_DEBUG=2 \
    CARGO_PROFILE_DEV_OPT_LEVEL=1 \
    CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=2 \
    RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes" \
    YARN_ENABLE_TELEMETRY=0
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      clang cmake pkg-config python3 libssl-dev \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src
RUN ln -sf /src/.yarn/releases/yarn-*.cjs /usr/local/bin/yarn \
    && yarn install --immutable --mode=skip-build \
    && cargo fetch

# Preserve dependencies, Cargo.lock, source, debug symbols and build outputs so
# the scanner can modify and rebuild the project without Internet access.
ENV CARGO_NET_OFFLINE=true \
    YARN_ENABLE_NETWORK=0
RUN yarn build \
    && yarn workspace @examples/napi build \
    && yarn workspace @examples/compat-mode build \
    && yarn workspace @examples/custom-async-runtime build \
    && yarn workspace @examples/shared-async-runtime build \
    && cargo test --workspace --no-run

# Small native smoke test; the full offline test commands are in threat_model.md.
RUN node -e "require('./examples/napi/index.cjs')"

# Builds Argo CD from the checkout at /src and keeps everything needed to build and test it offline:
# the Go module cache, the UI's node_modules, and the helm, kustomize and git-lfs versions that Argo CD ships with.
FROM docker.io/library/golang:1.27-trixie

ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 \
    GODEBUG=tarinsecurepath=0,zipinsecurepath=0 \
    COREPACK_ENABLE_DOWNLOAD_PROMPT=0

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      ca-certificates curl git gnupg gpg-agent openssh-client make unzip jq procps sudo \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Tests in reposerver/ and util/git create commits in temporary repositories and need a git identity.
RUN git config --system user.name "Argo CD Scanner" \
    && git config --system user.email "scanner@localhost"

# Node.js for the UI, from the official image (Argo CD's own Dockerfile builds the UI with Node 24).
COPY --from=docker.io/library/node:24-trixie /usr/local/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node
COPY --from=docker.io/library/node:24-trixie /usr/local/lib/node_modules /usr/local/lib/node_modules
RUN ln -s ../lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npm-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npm \
    && ln -s ../lib/node_modules/npm/bin/npx-cli.js /usr/local/bin/npx \
    && ln -s ../lib/node_modules/corepack/dist/corepack.js /usr/local/bin/corepack \
    && node --version

COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src

# helm, kustomize and git-lfs at the versions pinned (and checksum-verified) in hack/tool-versions.sh.
# The repo-server runs these tools to render manifests. The installers call sudo, as in the release Dockerfile.
RUN BIN=/usr/local/bin ./hack/install.sh helm kustomize git-lfs \
    && git lfs install --skip-repo --system

# The repo-server calls these wrappers for GnuPG and commit signature verification; the release image puts them on PATH.
RUN install -m 0755 hack/gpg-wrapper.sh hack/git-verify-wrapper.sh /usr/local/bin/

# Go dependencies for both modules (the repository root and the nested gitops-engine module). If go.mod asks for a
# newer Go than this image has, the toolchain is downloaded here and stays in the module cache for offline use.
RUN go mod download && (cd gitops-engine && go mod download)

# Argo CD ships one multi-call binary that picks its component from its name, as in the release images.
RUN go build -o /usr/local/bin/argocd ./cmd \
    && for name in argocd-server argocd-repo-server argocd-application-controller argocd-applicationset-controller \
         argocd-cmp-server argocd-commit-server argocd-notifications argocd-dex argocd-git-ask-pass argocd-k8s-auth; do \
         ln -s argocd "/usr/local/bin/$name"; \
       done \
    && argocd version --client --short

# Compile every non-test package once so later builds and reproducers are fast.
RUN go build ./... && (cd gitops-engine && go build ./...)

# UI dependencies, so the UI can be built and tested offline (pnpm version comes from ui/package.json).
RUN cd ui && corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile

# Baseline tests for the security-sensitive areas: auth/session/RBAC, the API server, and manifest generation.
# A failing test must not abort the build. The skipped tests expect permission errors, which root never gets.
RUN go test -short -p 4 -timeout 20m \
      -skip '^(TestDirectoryPermissionInitializer|TestInit)$|^Test_getPotentiallyValidManifests$/^unreadable_file_throws_error$' \
      ./util/session/... ./util/oidc/... ./util/rbac/... ./util/settings/... ./server/logout/... \
      ./server/application/... ./server/project/... ./reposerver/repository/... ./util/helm/... ./util/kustomize/... \
    || echo 'WARNING: baseline Go tests reported failures'

# Reproducers and patches must build with the network disabled.
ENV GOPROXY=off \
    GOSUMDB=off

CMD ["bash"]

# Threat model: cryptsetup / libcryptsetup

## What this project does

cryptsetup is the userspace side of Linux block-device encryption and integrity. It consists of:

- **libcryptsetup** (`lib/`) – the library that parses on-disk metadata, derives keys (PBKDF2,
  Argon2), unlocks keyslots and drives the kernel device-mapper targets `dm-crypt`, `dm-verity`
  and `dm-integrity`. It is linked by systemd (`systemd-cryptsetup`, `systemd-cryptenroll`,
  `systemd-veritysetup`, `systemd-homed`), udisks2, initramfs generators, installers and others.
- **CLI tools** (`src/`) – `cryptsetup`, `veritysetup`, `integritysetup`; thin wrappers over the
  library.
- **LUKS2 token plugins** (`tokens/`) – the optional `ssh` token plugin, loaded by `dlopen()`.

Supported on-disk formats: LUKS1, LUKS2 (binary header + JSON metadata, two copies), plain
dm-crypt, loop-AES keyfiles, TrueCrypt/VeraCrypt (TCRYPT), BitLocker (BITLK), Apple FileVault2
(FVAULT2), dm-verity superblock (+ FEC and root-hash signature), dm-integrity superblock, and the
LUKS2 SED OPAL extension.

The library almost always runs **as root**, very often automatically (udev rules, systemd units,
initramfs at boot, desktop auto-mount of removable media). A bug in metadata parsing is therefore
a bug in a root process that is fed attacker-shaped data with no user interaction.

## Where untrusted input enters

Treat everything read from a block device or a file passed as a device/header as
attacker-controlled. Concretely:

1. **On-disk metadata of every supported format** – LUKS1 header and keyslot areas; LUKS2 binary
   headers, both JSON metadata copies, keyslot areas and the header-selection/recovery logic;
   TCRYPT/VeraCrypt headers (including hidden/system volume variants, decrypted with the user's
   passphrase but otherwise attacker-shaped); BITLK metadata blocks, entries and FVE datums;
   FVAULT2 CoreStorage metadata; VERITY superblock, hash tree and FEC area; INTEGRITY superblock.
   Attack scenarios: a malicious USB stick or disk, a downloaded or cloud VM image, an
   "evil maid" who rewrites the header of a laptop disk, a compromised storage backend.
2. **Detached header files** (`--header`), **header backup files** (`luksHeaderRestore`), and
   **LUKS2 metadata imported via `cryptsetup token import` / `--json-file`**.
3. **LUKS2 JSON content that drives behaviour**: segments, digests, keyslot areas/offsets,
   reencryption state (`reencrypt` keyslot, hotzone, resilience mode, checksums), token
   definitions (including which external token plugin name is requested and the fields the
   `ssh` token reads: `ssh_server`, `ssh_user`, `ssh_path`, `ssh_keypath`), flags and
   requirements, labels/subsystem.
4. **Keyfiles and passphrases** – content is trusted (it comes from the user) but size and
   encoding handling (keyfile offset/size limits, UTF-8 / TCRYPT keyfile pooling, loop-AES
   keyfile parsing) must be robust.
5. **Data area contents during online reencryption** – the library reads and rewrites data in
   place, guided by header-controlled offsets and checksums.

Trusted (out of the attacker's control in this model): the command line and API caller,
the kernel and its device-mapper/crypto implementations, linked crypto libraries, json-c,
libblkid, libdevmapper, the external token plugin directory and the plugin `.so` files in it,
root-owned configuration, the kernel keyring of the calling user.

## What a real vulnerability looks like here

In scope (roughly in order of interest):

- **Memory-safety bugs** reachable from crafted metadata or header files: out-of-bounds
  read/write, use-after-free, double free, integer overflow leading to wrong allocation or
  offset, uninitialised memory used in a security decision, unbounded recursion/allocation.
- **Key or secret disclosure**: volume key, passphrase or derived key material leaked to logs,
  debug output, swap-able unlocked memory, other files, other users, or written to disk; key
  material left in memory after it is no longer needed when that is observable by a less
  privileged party.
- **Silent confidentiality/integrity downgrade** triggered by header tampering: a crafted header
  that, after the legitimate user unlocks with their passphrase, makes cryptsetup activate or
  reencrypt the device so that subsequently written data is stored in plaintext, under a key the
  attacker knows, or with integrity protection silently disabled (cf. CVE-2021-4122, where a
  forged reencryption state decrypted data in place). Null cipher acceptance in the wrong place
  falls here.
- **Root-process side effects driven by metadata**: e.g. a header causing a root process to read
  or send an arbitrary local file, load an unexpected plugin, or open
  network connections without the user asking for that token.
- **Wrong cryptography**: incorrect KDF/cipher parameters accepted or computed, keyslot
  verification bypass (unlocking without the correct passphrase), digest checks that can be
  skipped, weak-parameter acceptance that bypasses documented minimums.

## Known design limits (do not report as vulnerabilities)

- LUKS metadata is **checksummed, not authenticated**. Anyone who can write the header can
  destroy it, swap in another header, lower PBKDF cost for *new* keyslots, rename tokens or
  change labels. These are not bugs **unless** they lead to one of the in-scope outcomes above
  (memory corruption, key disclosure, silent plaintext/known-key writes, out-of-bounds writes,
  keyslot bypass).
- Denial of service by corrupting or deleting the header (the volume will not open) is expected.
- An attacker with write access to the **data area** can corrupt or replay ciphertext; dm-crypt
  does not provide integrity unless `--integrity` / AEAD is configured.
- Physical attacks on a running unlocked system, cold-boot, DMA, kernel memory disclosure,
  hardware/firmware flaws in SED OPAL drives, and timing side channels of the underlying crypto
  libraries are out of scope.
- Passphrase strength and user choice of weak parameters on the command line.
- Anything requiring the attacker to control the command line, environment of a root process,
  the plugin directory, or `/etc` is out of scope.

## Components that matter most / least

Highest priority:
- `lib/`
  The bundled reference implementation in `lib/crypto_backend/argon2/` is **not built** in the
  scanner image (Argon2 comes from OpenSSL); findings only there are lower priority.

Medium:
- `tokens/ssh/` (experimental, but runs as root and reads header-supplied fields).
- `src/` CLI argument parsing and keyfile reading (input is trusted, but size/overflow bugs still
  count).

Low / out of scope:
- `tests/`, `tests/fuzz/` harnesses, `scripts/`, `misc/`, `docs/`, `po/`, `man/`, build files.

## How to exercise it (inside the scanner image)

Build outputs (both use the OpenSSL crypto backend, OpenSSL 3.5 with its Argon2 KDF; neither
the bundled Argon2 nor libargon2 is used):
- `/src/build/` – reference build (gcc, `-O2 -g`), tools in `/src/build/src/`.
- `/src/build-asan/` – clang ASan+UBSan build, tools in `/src/build-asan/src/`, libFuzzer
  targets in `/src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/`. `ASAN_OPTIONS`/`UBSAN_OPTIONS` are preset to abort
  on the first error. **Confirm memory-safety findings with the ASan build.**

Metadata parsing works on plain image files without root or device-mapper (luksDump,
bitlkDump, fvault2Dump).

Fuzzers (LUKS2 header with checksum fix-up, LUKS2 on-disk JSON, VERITY/INTEGRITY):

```sh
/src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/crypt2_load_fuzz -dict=/src/tests/fuzz/crypt2_load_fuzz.dict CORPUS/
/src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/crypt2_load_ondisk_fuzz -dict=/src/tests/fuzz/crypt2_load_ondisk_fuzz.dict CORPUS/
/src/build-asan/tests/fuzz/crypt_load_misc_fuzz CORPUS/
```

Library-level reproducers can be small C programs linked against
`/src/build-asan/lib/libcryptsetup.so`. API-level tests:
`/src/build/tests/api-test`, `api-test-2` (need root + device-mapper).

Activation, reencryption, verity/integrity format and most of `meson test -C /src/build` need
root, device-mapper, loop devices and sometimes `scsi_debug`; run them only inside the
privileged scanner VM. Tests that need networking (`ssh-test-plugin`) will not work offline.

## How we rate severity

- **Critical**: memory corruption with demonstrated or very likely code execution from a crafted
  header/image reachable without the passphrase (e.g. on `crypt_load()`, `isLuks`, `*Dump`,
  automatic probing by systemd/udisks); keyslot unlock without the correct passphrase;
  disclosure of the volume key to an unprivileged party.
- **High**: any out-of-bounds write, use-after-free or double free reachable from crafted
  metadata (default for memory corruption without a working exploit); crafted header that after
  a legitimate unlock causes silent plaintext or attacker-known-key writes or disables integrity;
  metadata/reencryption writes outside the device or header bounds; header-restore/lock-file
  races that write or leak arbitrary root-owned files.
- **Medium**: out-of-bounds read with limited information disclosure; key material left in
  memory/logs that is reachable only by root or after compromise; header fields making a root
  process read local files or open connections (token plugins); bugs reachable only after the
  correct passphrase is entered with a crafted header (lower one level when the crafted header
  requires prior write access to the specific victim device *and* user interaction).
- **Low**: crashes from NULL dereference, assertions, unbounded-but-finite CPU/memory use from
  crafted metadata (DoS), leaks on CLI error paths, undefined behaviour without demonstrated
  impact.
- Bugs only reachable by a trusted root caller passing nonsensical CLI/API arguments: Low or
  informational.

## How we would like reports and patches

- Target the `main` branch (`gitlab.com/cryptsetup/cryptsetup`).
- Include a minimal reproducer: preferably a script that generates the crafted image
  (like `tests/generators/`), otherwise a small xz-compressed image, plus the exact command and
  the ASan/UBSan output from `/src/build-asan`.
- State which formats and entry points are affected (`crypt_load` only? needs passphrase? needs
  root/dm?) and the first affected release if known.
- Patches: Linux kernel coding style (tabs), minimal and focused, no unrelated cleanups; fix the
  validation at the parsing/validation layer (e.g. `LUKS2_hdr_validate()` and friends) rather than
  adding checks at a single use site where possible. A regression test (new `tests/generators`
  image for `luks2-validation-test`, or an addition to the relevant `*-compat-test`) is
  appreciated.

## Anything to leave alone

- Do not report the lack of header authentication itself, PBKDF parameter choices, or
  deprecated-but-supported legacy formats/ciphers as vulnerabilities.
- Do not report issues only in the test suite, fuzz harnesses, or `misc/`/`scripts/` helpers.
- Do not report findings that depend on a modified kernel, malicious crypto library, or a
  malicious token plugin installed by root.
- Warnings about meson being "experimental" are expected.

# A pure TypeScript cryptography library from paulmillr's noble family, built and tested the way its CI
# (paulmillr/jsbt .github/workflows/test.yml) does: submodules, npm ci --ignore-scripts, tsc, node test/index.ts.
FROM node:24-trixie
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive \
    CI=true
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates git \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# scanner contract: the checkout lives inside the image, at /src
COPY . /src
WORKDIR /src

# The scanner clones without submodules. Some packages keep their test vectors (acvp-vectors) in one; fetch
# them now, while online. This is a no-op for packages without a .gitmodules.
RUN git config --global --add safe.directory '*' \
    && git submodule update --init --depth 1

# Install-time scripts of dependencies stay blocked, as in CI. `npm run build` is tsc; it emits the .js and
# .d.ts files that the published package ships.
RUN npm ci --ignore-scripts
RUN npm run build

# The fast test suite. Slow suites (npm run test:slow etc.) are left for the scanner to run when needed.
RUN npm test || echo "WARNING: npm test reported failures"

# Threat model

## What this project does and where untrusted input enters

Tinyauth is a lightweight authentication and authorization server for self-hosted applications. It can act as authentication middleware or as a standalone authentication server, with support for OAuth, LDAP, and access controls. It integrates with reverse proxies such as Traefik, Nginx, and Caddy.

Tinyauth has two core components: an OpenID Connect server and a set of forward-auth handlers.

The OpenID Connect server operates according to a standardized protocol, but incoming requests must never be assumed to be valid or specification-compliant. All input is untrusted and must be validated before use.

The forward-auth handlers receive requests from different proxies using different headers and conventions, without a single standardized interface. All incoming data must be treated as untrusted and validated before making security decisions, such as allowing or denying access.

## Security-critical components

### OpenID Connect server

The OpenID Connect server must follow the specification as closely as possible and fail closed when required validation fails. Although the protocol is standardized, its inputs remain untrusted, and implementation errors can compromise authentication or authorization.

### Forward-auth handlers

The forward-auth handlers require particular attention. Each proxy integration relies on different headers and request conventions. Attacker-controlled headers or other request data must not be mistaken for trusted proxy context or authentication information.

When reviewing these handlers, consider how the proxy constructs the request, which values an attacker can influence, and how Tinyauth validates those values before using them.

### Access-control service

The access-control service is closely tied to forward-auth. Its decisions depend on the request context supplied by the proxy. Injected or malformed values can cause access controls to incorrectly allow or deny a request.

Reviewing this service also requires considering the Docker and Kubernetes services, which provide access-control configuration.

### Session management and account handling

Session management and account handling are also security-critical. This includes the creation, validation, and expiration of sessions, along with authentication and identity handling for local bcrypt users, OAuth users, LDAP users, and Tailscale users.

## How to exercise it

See the `AGENTS.md` file for the available make commands. You can build the Tinyauth binary with the provided make commands and run it with a `.env` derived from the `.env.example`. You cannot however spin up a Docker stack so you will have to work with CLI commands (you have `curl` available) or Go test files.

To test the code directly, including against mock providers, refer to the existing `*_test.go` files for examples of the testing approach used in Tinyauth.

## How to assess severity

Assess severity based on demonstrated impact and exploitability. The following categories serve as guidelines.

### Critical

- Injection of attacker-controlled values into the trusted proxy context.
- Flaws in access-control evaluation that can bypass access restrictions.
- Bypasses of the OpenID Connect authorization flow.
- Bypasses of local, OAuth, LDAP, or Tailscale authentication.

### High

- Incorrect escaping or unescaping of security-sensitive values.
- Incorrect validation of URLs, paths, or other security-sensitive inputs.
- Incorrect generation of security-sensitive values, such as session cookies or OpenID Connect tokens and identifiers.

### Medium

- Cross-site request forgery (CSRF).
- Check-then-act race conditions.
- User enumeration.
- Denial of service (DoS).

## Intentional deviations

Do not report an intentional, clearly documented deviation from a specification solely because it is noncompliant.

A documented deviation remains in scope if it introduces a security vulnerability.

# Argo CD threat model

Argo CD is a declarative GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. It watches Git, Helm and OCI
repositories, renders Kubernetes manifests from them, and syncs those manifests into one or more
Kubernetes clusters. It holds credentials for those clusters and for the repositories, so a flaw can
lead to cluster takeover or credential theft across many environments.

Project security policy: https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md
Operator security notes: `docs/operator-manual/security.md`, `docs/operator-manual/applicationset/Security.md`

## Components and where untrusted input enters

All components are built from one binary (`cmd/main.go`) and selected by name.

- **argocd-server** (`server/`, `util/session`, `util/oidc`, `util/rbac`, `util/settings`): gRPC and
  REST/gRPC-gateway API, the web UI, SSO login/callback/logout, webhooks (`util/webhook`), and the
  application and terminal proxies. This is the main network-facing component. Treat every HTTP/gRPC
  request, header, cookie, JWT, OIDC response and webhook payload as attacker-controlled.
- **argocd-repo-server** (`reposerver/`, `util/git`, `util/helm`, `util/kustomize`, `util/app/discovery`,
  `util/io`): clones repositories and renders manifests by running git, helm, kustomize and config
  management plugins. Treat repository *contents* as attacker-controlled: anyone with write access to
  any tracked repository can supply them. It must not escape the repository or application path,
  read other repositories' files or the server's files, or execute arbitrary commands.
- **argocd-application-controller** (`controller/`, `gitops-engine/`): reconciles and syncs resources
  into clusters using stored cluster credentials. Rendered manifests and live cluster state are input.
- **argocd-applicationset-controller** (`applicationset/`): generates Applications from generators
  (Git, SCM providers, pull requests, cluster lists, plugins). Data returned by SCM providers and Git
  is untrusted, and generated Applications must stay within the AppProject constraints.
- **argocd-commit-server** (`commitserver/`): writes hydrated manifests back to Git.
- **argocd-cmp-server** (`cmpserver/`): runs config management plugins as sidecars.
- **argocd-notifications** (`notification_controller/`): sends notifications using templates.
- **CLI** (`cmd/argocd`): runs on user machines and talks to the API server. A malicious or
  compromised API server is a valid attacker for CLI bugs (e.g. local file writes or command execution).
- **UI** (`ui/`, React/TypeScript): renders resource names, annotations, manifests, logs, links and
  other data that originate from Git or from clusters. Stored or reflected XSS through that data is in scope.

## Attackers to consider

- Unauthenticated network clients of argocd-server.
- Authenticated users with limited RBAC permissions: read-only users, users scoped to one AppProject,
  and project-scoped automation tokens. The core security boundary is **RBAC and AppProject
  restrictions** (allowed source repos, destination clusters and namespaces, resource allow/deny lists,
  `sourceNamespaces` for apps in any namespace). Any way for such a user to act outside their
  permissions or project is in scope.
- Users with write access to a Git/Helm/OCI repository that some Application tracks, but no Argo CD
  permissions.
- Senders of webhook requests and responders to outbound requests (SCM APIs, OIDC providers, Helm/OCI
  registries).

## Trusted / out of scope

- Argo CD administrators and anyone who can change `argocd-cm`, `argocd-rbac-cm`, `argocd-secret`,
  `argocd-cmd-params-cm` or the Argo CD namespace. They are fully trusted.
- Anyone with direct Kubernetes API access to create or modify Argo CD CRDs in the Argo CD namespace.
- Config management plugins themselves: they are operator-installed code and can run anything.
- Documented risks in `docs/operator-manual/security.md`, for example that a user with write access to
  a tracked repository can change what gets deployed, or that helm/kustomize may follow remote bases and
  chart dependencies. Report these only if they bypass a documented restriction (e.g. reading files
  outside the repository, escaping AppProject source/destination limits).
- Vulnerabilities in dependencies (helm, kustomize, git, Go modules, npm packages) that are not
  reachable through Argo CD code. Dependency CVEs reported only from a version number are out of scope.
- `test/`, `hack/`, `docs/` and `examples/`, and e2e test fixtures.

## How to exercise it

- Unit tests sit next to the code (`go test ./server/...`, `./reposerver/...`, `./util/...`,
  `./controller/...`, `./applicationset/...`). Many API server tests build an in-memory server with fake
  Kubernetes clients; `server/application/application_test.go` and `server/server_test.go` show how.
- Manifest generation can be driven directly through `reposerver/repository` tests, which have
  fixtures under `reposerver/repository/testdata` and `util/helm/testdata`.
- helm, kustomize and git-lfs are installed at the versions Argo CD ships with.
- The UI's dependencies are installed in `ui/node_modules`; `cd ui && pnpm test` runs its tests.
- There is no Kubernetes cluster in the image. Prefer reproducers as Go unit tests.
- The image runs as root, so tests that expect permission-denied errors (`TestDirectoryPermissionInitializer`,
  `TestInit` and `Test_getPotentiallyValidManifests/unreadable_file_throws_error` in `reposerver/repository`)
  fail there. That is expected and not a finding; Argo CD components run as a non-root user (UID 999) in production.
- The scan has no network access, so tests that fetch remote content (for example `TestGenerateHelmWithURL`,
  which downloads a Helm values file from GitHub) fail. That is also expected and not a finding.

## How we rate severity

We use CVSS 3.1 and publish advisories through GitHub Security Advisories. As guidance:

- **Critical**: unauthenticated remote code execution, authentication bypass on argocd-server, or
  obtaining cluster or repository credentials without authentication.
- **High**: an authenticated low-privilege user (or a holder of a project token) gaining admin
  privileges, deploying outside their AppProject's allowed destinations, sources or resource kinds,
  or reading secrets they are not authorized to see; code execution or arbitrary file read on the
  repo-server driven by repository contents; stored XSS in the UI from repository or cluster data.
- **Medium**: information disclosure of non-secret data across projects, open redirects, CSRF on
  state-changing endpoints, denial of service of a component by an authenticated user.
- **Low**: denial of service that needs administrator-controlled configuration, or issues that need an
  unusual, insecure configuration that the docs warn against.

## How we would like reports

Keep reports short. Please include the affected component, the attacker's required access (none,
read-only user, project member, repository writer), and a reproducer, ideally as a Go unit test.
Please validate impact before reporting, and don't report theoretical issues without a concrete path
from attacker input to impact.

# Threat model: noble-ciphers

## What this project does and where untrusted input enters
Audited and minimal JS implementation of symmetric ciphers: Salsa20, ChaCha20, XSalsa20, XChaCha20, Poly1305, ChaCha20-Poly1305, AES (ECB, CBC, CTR, CFB, GCM, GCM-SIV, SIV, KW, KWP, CMAC), POLYVAL/GHASH, FF1 and the `managedNonce` helper.

It is a library: it has no network listener, no CLI and no file I/O. Untrusted input arrives through its public
API, called by applications in Node.js, Deno, Bun and browsers. Assume every byte array, hex string, bigint,
number and options object passed to an exported function may be attacker-controlled, unless the README documents
that argument as trusted (for example a secret key generated by the caller).

## Components that matter most / least
- AEAD decryption with attacker-controlled ciphertext, tag and AAD: tag verification, length checks,
  truncated or empty inputs, anything that returns plaintext for a forged tag.
- `aes.ts` (all modes, padding handling in CBC/ECB), `chacha.ts`, `salsa.ts`, `_arx.ts`, `_poly1305.ts`,
  `_polyval.ts`, `ff1.ts`, `utils.ts` (`managedNonce`, buffer helpers, `output` buffer reuse).
- Counter overflow and keystream reuse, output-buffer aliasing (`encrypt(data, out)` where out overlaps
  input), and in-place operation.
- `webcrypto.ts` is a thin wrapper; bugs in how it forwards arguments are in scope.

## How to exercise it
- Source is TypeScript under `src/`; `npm run build` (tsc) emits the shipped .js next to it. Tests import the
  built output via package exports, so rebuild after editing source.
- `npm test` runs the fast suite (`node test/index.ts`); individual files run with `node test/<name>.test.ts`.
- Test vectors (Wycheproof, ACVP, RFC/KAT) are under `test/vectors/` (ACVP vectors come from the `test/vectors/acvp-vectors` submodule). Reproducers are best written
  as a small `node repro.ts` script that imports the package by path and compares against a vector or a
  reference implementation.
- Slow suite: `npm run test:slow`.

## How you rate severity
- **Critical**: an attacker who controls only public inputs (signatures, public keys, ciphertexts, messages,
  encoded points) can recover a secret key, forge a signature/MAC/tag, or decrypt; or a valid output is
  produced for the wrong input in a way an application relies on (e.g. `verify` returns true for an invalid
  signature).
- **High**: incorrect output for valid inputs (wrong hash/ciphertext/shared secret, non-interoperable
  results), accepting malformed or non-canonical encodings where the spec requires rejection (malleability),
  missing input validation that lets a caller silently get insecure results, or nonce/randomness misuse
  inside the library.
- **Medium**: timing differences on secret data that are measurable in a realistic harness and are not one of
  the documented limitations below; prototype pollution or option-object confusion reachable through the API.
- **Low**: denial of service through unbounded CPU or memory on attacker-controlled sizes, when the
  parameter is something an application would plausibly pass through from an attacker; exceptions of the
  wrong type or with confusing messages.
- A finding needs a reproducer that runs against the built package. Report the spec, RFC or test vector the
  behaviour violates.

## Anything to leave alone
- Constant-time execution is a goal at the algorithm level only. JIT, garbage collection and bigint
  arithmetic make strict constant-time impossible in JavaScript; do not report generic "JS is not
  constant-time" or "bigints are not zeroized" issues.
- Secrets staying in memory (immutable strings and bigints, buffers not zeroized, values held across `await`)
  are documented and out of scope.
- The quality of `crypto.getRandomValues` is out of scope.
- `benchmark/`, `test/`, `audit/` and dev dependencies (jsbt, prettier, typescript, bismar, fast-check) do not
  ship to users and are out of scope, except where a test itself is wrong and hides a real bug.
- Please keep patches minimal, in the existing code style, and add a regression test next to the related
  tests.
- AES uses T-tables, which leak cache timing; this is documented. Nonce reuse by the caller is a caller error, unless the library's own API (e.g. `managedNonce`) causes it.

# Grafana OSS threat model for scanner reports

## Scope

Scan the open-source code in `grafana/grafana`, including its Go server, HTTP APIs, frontend, bundled plugins, and application modules. Treat Grafana Cloud services and private Enterprise code that is absent from this repository as out of scope. A finding must identify the affected code, required configuration or feature flags, and the attacker position.

## Trust boundaries

- Browser clients and API callers supply requests, authentication material, dashboard and panel content, queries, and provisioning inputs. Check authentication, authorization, and organization/resource scope at the server endpoint that processes each action.
- Grafana stores and uses data-source credentials and other secrets. Check whether lower-privilege users, plugins, or data-source responses can read them or cause Grafana to send them to an unintended destination.
- Data sources, plugins, and imported dashboards can supply untrusted content that reaches the browser or server. Check output encoding and sanitization in the actual rendering path, as well as server-side request and file boundaries.
- Cross-organization and cross-user access, role or permission changes, and server-side requests to internal destinations are high-value cases. Do not infer exploitability from a missing check in isolation; trace the reachable route and its other guards.

## Report requirements

Provide a reproducible request or UI sequence, the lowest privileges needed, relevant settings and feature flags, the observed outcome, and a proposed patch where possible. Distinguish source-level possibilities from a demonstrated result. Do not include live credentials or customer data in a report.

The image retains `/src`, the built Grafana binary under `bin/`, frontend assets under `public/`, Go modules, and Yarn dependencies. Run focused Go tests with `go test` and frontend tests with `yarn jest --runInBand --watch=false` from `/src`; start the server with a local test configuration when an end-to-end reproducer is needed. The scanner environment has no Internet access after the image build.

# Threat model

## What this project does and where untrusted input enters

sccache is a ccache-like compiler cache written in Rust. The `sccache` binary wraps a compiler
invocation (C/C++, Rust, CUDA, HIP, MSVC, ...), hashes the inputs, and either returns a cached
artifact or runs the real compiler and stores the result. The same binary acts as a thin client
and as a long-lived per-user server that does the work. It also ships `sccache-dist`, a scheduler
and build server for distributed compilation.

Untrusted input enters in these places:

- **Cache contents.** Remote caches (S3, GCS, Azure, Redis, Memcached, WebDAV, GitHub Actions,
  OSS, COS) are often shared by many machines and CI jobs, and anyone with write access to the
  bucket can put entries there. Treat every entry read from storage as hostile. sccache unpacks
  entries (zip and compressed blobs, see `src/cache/cache_io.rs` and `src/cache/`) and writes the
  object files, dep files, stderr and so on to paths on disk. Path traversal or writing outside
  the expected output paths, symlink tricks, and memory corruption or panics while decoding are
  in scope. So are crashes and hangs on malformed entries. Note that a malicious entry can always
  hold a malicious *object file* for the expected output path. That is a known limitation of a
  shared cache with untrusted writers, not a finding on its own.
- **Cache key computation.** Two compilations that produce different output must not share a
  key. Anything that leaves out an input affecting the output (an argument, an env var, an
  included file, the compiler binary, `SCCACHE_BASEDIRS` normalization, preprocessor "direct
  mode" in `src/compiler/preprocessor_cache.rs`) so that an attacker can get their artifact
  served for someone else's compilation is in scope (cache poisoning).
- **Compiler command lines and source files.** The argument parsers in `src/compiler/` (`args.rs`,
  `gcc.rs`, `clang.rs`, `msvc.rs`, `nvcc.rs`, `rust.rs`, ...) parse arguments, response files
  (`@file`) and dep-info / preprocessor output written by the compiler. Build systems pass these
  from project files, so they can come from an untrusted repository. sccache must not run a
  command or write a file that the plain compiler invocation would not have.
- **The local client/server protocol** (`src/protocol.rs`, `src/server.rs`). The server listens
  on `127.0.0.1:4226` by default (or a Unix socket with `SCCACHE_SERVER_UDS`) and runs compilers
  with the argv, cwd and environment the client sends. There is no peer authentication, so on a
  multi-user host another local user can connect. Report problems in decoding these messages
  (crashes, excessive allocation). Report privilege issues only with a concrete multi-user
  scenario and an explanation of why it goes beyond the documented design.
- **Distributed compilation** (`src/dist/`, `src/bin/sccache-dist/`). The scheduler and build
  servers accept HTTP requests from clients and from each other, authenticated with tokens or
  JWTs (`DANGEROUSLY_INSECURE` exists and is out of scope). Build servers receive toolchain
  tarballs and input archives from clients and run the compiler inside bubblewrap with an overlay
  filesystem (`build.rs`) or a Docker container. Escaping the sandbox, writing outside the build
  directory while unpacking toolchains or inputs, authentication bypass, one client reading or
  tampering with another client's job or toolchain, and pre-auth crashes are all in scope. The
  client side must also treat results returned by a build server as untrusted (output paths in
  particular).
- **Configuration.** The config file and `SCCACHE_*` environment variables are trusted. Exposing
  credentials from config (cloud keys, dist tokens) in logs, stats output, error messages or
  network traffic to an unintended host is in scope.

## Components that matter most / least

- Most important: `src/cache/` (especially entry decoding and writing outputs), the cache key
  logic in `src/compiler/compiler.rs`, `c.rs`, `rust.rs` and `preprocessor_cache.rs`,
  `src/dist/` and `src/bin/sccache-dist/`, `src/server.rs` and `src/protocol.rs`.
- Also in scope: the per-compiler argument parsers, `src/lru_disk_cache/`, `src/util.rs`,
  `src/config.rs`, `src/dist/client_auth.rs` (OAuth flow with a local HTTP listener).
- Less important: `src/jobserver.rs`, the stats and CLI formatting code.
- Out of scope: `benches/`, `tests/` (fixtures and harness), `scripts/`, `snap/`, `docs/`,
  `flake.nix`, and third-party crates unless sccache uses them in an unsafe way.

## How to exercise it

- Everything is pre-built in `/src/target/debug`: `sccache` (all default storage backends and the
  dist client) and `sccache-dist`. Rebuild offline with `cargo build --offline --locked` and
  `cargo build --offline --locked --features dist-server --bin sccache-dist`.
- gcc, clang and rustc are installed so real compilations can be cached. A quick loop:
  `SCCACHE_DIR=/tmp/cache SCCACHE_START_SERVER=1 SCCACHE_NO_DAEMON=1 SCCACHE_LOG=debug ./target/debug/sccache`
  in one shell, then `./target/debug/sccache gcc -c tests/test.c -o /tmp/t.o` in another. The
  local disk cache in `SCCACHE_DIR` is the easiest way to plant crafted cache entries.
- `redis-server` and `memcached` are installed for testing those backends locally, for example
  `redis-server --daemonize yes` and `SCCACHE_REDIS_ENDPOINT=redis://127.0.0.1:6379`.
- Tests: `cargo test --offline --locked --lib --bins --tests -- --test-threads 1`. Integration
  tests start a real sccache server and must run one at a time. The `dist-tests` feature builds
  `tests/dist.rs`, which needs Docker and is not usable in this image.
- `sccache-dist` can be run locally with a token-auth scheduler and build server config (see
  `docs/Distributed.md`). The bubblewrap builder needs root or user namespaces.

## How you rate severity

- Critical: code execution on a machine that only *reads* from a shared cache (beyond receiving a
  malicious object file, see above), escaping the sccache-dist sandbox to run code on the build
  server host, or authentication bypass on the scheduler/build server leading to code execution.
- High: writing files outside the intended output paths from a cache entry or dist result;
  cache-key collisions that let an attacker serve their artifact for a different compilation;
  one dist client tampering with another client's builds; leaking cloud or dist credentials.
- Medium: denial of service of the sccache server or the dist scheduler/build server from
  untrusted input (panics, hangs, unbounded memory), and information leaks between dist jobs.
- Low: issues that need control of trusted configuration, or of the same user account that runs
  the sccache server.

## Anything to leave alone

- Do not report that the `DANGEROUSLY_INSECURE` auth modes are insecure.
- Do not report that a writer to a shared cache can store a bad object file for the matching key.
- Do not report that the configured compiler or a `SCCACHE_*` variable runs arbitrary programs;
  the user picked them.
- Do not report that the local server listens on TCP localhost by default; that is documented.
  Problems that follow from it (see above) are fine to report with a concrete scenario.
- Proposed patches should keep the cache key format stable unless the fix needs a change, and
  should say so when they change it (it invalidates every existing cache).

name: "Terms"
# An enrolment pull request must accept the OSS Scanner terms: the box in the pull request template, ticked in the
# description. This check fails until it is, and runs again whenever the description is edited.
#
# pull_request_target, not pull_request: with pull_request the workflow file is taken from the pull request itself, so
# a contributor could edit this check away. This job reads only the event's description, never the pull request's
# code, and gets no token at all. The description reaches the script through an environment variable, never by
# ${{ }} substitution into the script, so its text cannot become shell.
on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, edited, reopened, synchronize]

permissions: {}

jobs:
  terms-accepted:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 2
    steps:
      - name: The description accepts the OSS Scanner terms
        env:
          BODY: ${{ github.event.pull_request.body }}
          AUTHOR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.user.login }}
        run: |
          # The repository's maintainers and bots (as in cla.yaml's allowlist) do not enrol through this form.
          case "$AUTHOR" in
            carlini|srxzr-ant|punitshah|dependabot\[bot\]|github-actions\[bot\])
              echo "Opened by $AUTHOR, a maintainer or bot of this repository: no terms box needed."; exit 0 ;;
          esac
          if printf '%s\n' "$BODY" | grep -qiE '^[[:space:]]*[-*][[:space:]]+\[[xX]\][[:space:]]+I accept the \[OSS Scanner terms\]\(https://red\.anthropic\.com/oss-scanner/terms/?\)'; then
            echo "The OSS Scanner terms are accepted in the description."
          else
            echo "::error::Tick 'I accept the OSS Scanner terms' in the pull request description. Editing the description runs this check again."
            exit 1
          fi

name: "CLA Assistant"
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, closed, reopened, synchronize]

permissions:
  actions: write
  checks: read
  contents: write
  pull-requests: write
  statuses: write

jobs:
  CLAAssistant:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - name: "CLA Assistant"
        # contains() rather than == so the action also fires when the sign
        # phrase or `recheck` is accompanied by a small amount of extra text;
        # the action itself enforces the precise matching policy.
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request_target' || contains(github.event.comment.body, 'recheck') || contains(github.event.comment.body, 'I have read the CLA Document and I hereby sign the CLA')
        # Upstream contributor-assistant/github-action was archived 2026-03-23
        # still on Node 20 (deprecated 2026-06-02). This fork bumps to Node 24
        # and adds: an impersonation guard (PR opener must be an author or
        # co-author of at least one commit), Co-authored-by trailer support,
        # email-based allowlist matching, automatic retry of transient
        # GitHub 5xx errors, and actionable unlinked-email guidance.
        uses: iainmcgin/cla-github-action@0d27e5a16278d4adb6b0c4b92f08ad27b0a21dc8 # v3.2.0 (sha-pinned)
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        with:
          path-to-document: "https://github.com/${{ github.repository }}/blob/${{ github.event.repository.default_branch }}/CLA.md"
          path-to-signatures: "signatures/cla.json"
          branch: "cla-signatures"
          # noreply@anthropic.com is the email AI assistants use on Co-authored-by
          # trailers; allowlisting it suppresses that synthetic co-author, and the
          # PR opener still has to sign. Bots cannot sign a CLA.
          allowlist: "carlini,srxzr-ant,punitshah,dependabot[bot],github-actions[bot],noreply@anthropic.com"

name: "Build"
# Builds the project an enrolment pull request adds or changes, with tools/check. The output is in the run's log.
# A failure is not a verdict: this runner is much smaller than the scanner's build machine (tools/check_build.py).
#
# pull_request_target, not pull_request, so the pull request cannot edit this workflow or tools/check:
#   - The checkout is the base branch, never the pull request.
#   - The pull request may only change files directly inside one projects/<name>/, or the check fails.
#   - Only those files are taken from it, as regular files written from git's object store.
#   - Its Dockerfile runs only inside `docker build`, never as a step on the runner.
#
# This job builds code from anyone. Never add a secret, a cache, an artifact or a write permission to it.
# Runs do not wait for a maintainer's approval. To build only on request, remove pull_request_target below.
#
# To build a pull request by number:
#   gh workflow run build.yaml -f pr=123

run-name: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title || format('Pull request {0}', inputs.pr) }}

on:
  pull_request_target:
    types: [opened, reopened, synchronize]
    paths: ["projects/**"]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      pr:
        description: "Number of the pull request to build"
        required: true
        type: number

permissions: {}

concurrency:
  group: build-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || inputs.pr }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  project-builds:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # tools/check allows the build 45 minutes.
    timeout-minutes: 60
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 (sha-pinned)
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - name: Take projects/<name>/ from the pull request, and nothing else
        id: project
        timeout-minutes: 5
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number || inputs.pr }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          export LC_ALL=C  # a-z below is ASCII only

          fail() { echo "::error::$1"; exit 1; }

          [[ $PR =~ ^[0-9]+$ ]] || fail "Not a pull request number."
          pull=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR")
          sha=$(jq -r .head.sha <<< "$pull")
          [[ $sha =~ ^[0-9a-f]{40}$ ]] || fail "Could not read the pull request's head commit."
          # Only one page of changed files is read below.
          [ "$(jq -r .changed_files <<< "$pull")" -le 100 ] || fail "This pull request changes more than 100 files."

          # Every changed path, a renamed file under both names, must be directly inside one projects/<name>/.
          gh api "repos/$REPO/pulls/$PR/files?per_page=100" --jq '.[] | .filename, (.previous_filename // empty)' > "$RUNNER_TEMP/paths"
          name="" outside=0
          while IFS= read -r path; do
            if [[ $path =~ ^projects/([^/]+)/[^/]+$ ]]; then
              [[ -z $name || $name == "${BASH_REMATCH[1]}" ]] || fail "This pull request changes more than one project. One project per pull request."
              name=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}
              continue
            fi
            outside=1
            # Print only plain paths: the runner could read any other as a workflow command.
            [[ $path =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9._/-]+$ ]] && echo "outside projects/<name>/: $path" || echo "outside projects/<name>/: (a path with unusual characters)"
          done < "$RUNNER_TEMP/paths"

          if [ -z "$name" ]; then
            echo "This pull request changes no project: nothing to build."
            exit 0
          fi
          # Same rule as NAME in tools/validate.py.
          [[ $name =~ ^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]{0,62}$ ]] || fail "The directory name under projects/ must be a-z 0-9 . _ - (starting with a letter or digit, at most 63)."
          [ "$outside" = 0 ] || fail "This pull request changes files outside projects/$name/ (listed above). An enrolment changes nothing else."

          # Fetch the pull request's commit. Nothing is checked out.
          git fetch --quiet --no-tags --depth=1 origin "$sha"
          git ls-tree -r -z "$sha" -- "projects/$name/" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/tree"
          if [ ! -s "$RUNNER_TEMP/tree" ]; then
            echo "This pull request removes projects/$name/: nothing to build."
            exit 0
          fi

          # Replace projects/<name>/ with the pull request's files.
          rm -rf "projects/$name"
          mkdir "projects/$name"
          while IFS= read -r -d '' entry; do
            read -r mode _ blob <<< "${entry%%$'\t'*}"
            file=${entry#*$'\t'}
            file=${file#"projects/$name/"}
            # 100644 and 100755 are regular files. A file in a subdirectory has a / in its name.
            if [[ $mode != 100644 && $mode != 100755 ]] || ! [[ $file =~ ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$ ]]; then
              fail "projects/$name/ may hold only regular files with plain names: no directories, symbolic links or submodules."
            fi
            git cat-file blob "$blob" > "projects/$name/$file"
          done < "$RUNNER_TEMP/tree"

          echo "Building projects/$name/ as it is at $sha:"
          ls -l "projects/$name"
          echo "name=$name" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "sha=$sha" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - name: Make room and install PyYAML
        if: steps.project.outputs.name != ''
        run: |
          # Unused toolchains, removed to free disk for the build.
          sudo rm -rf /usr/share/dotnet /usr/local/lib/android /opt/ghc /opt/hostedtoolcache/CodeQL
          df -h /
          python3 -c 'import yaml' 2>/dev/null || { sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y -qq python3-yaml; }

      - name: Build the project with tools/check
        if: steps.project.outputs.name != ''
        env:
          NAME: ${{ steps.project.outputs.name }}
          SHA: ${{ steps.project.outputs.sha }}
        run: |
          # Until the token is printed again, the runner reads none of the build's output as a workflow command.
          resume="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
          echo "::stop-commands::$resume"
          code=0
          python3 tools/check --no-shell "$NAME" < /dev/null || code=$?
          echo "::$resume::"

          case $code in
            0) result="builds" ;;
            1) result="does not build (the log says which step failed)" ;;
            2) result="breaks the enrolment rules (the log lists them)" ;;
            *) result="could not be checked: tools/check exited $code" ;;
          esac
          echo "\`projects/$NAME/\` at \`${SHA:0:7}\` $result." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
          [ "$code" = 0 ] || echo "::error::projects/$NAME/ $result."
          exit "$code"

name: "Triage"
# Comments on an enrolment pull request with what a reviewer would otherwise look up by hand: the project's stars,
# forks, license and criticality score, where its packages stand among the most downloaded on PyPI, npm and
# crates.io, whether whoever opened it looks like an active maintainer, whether its SECURITY.md and its OSS-Fuzz
# project (if it has one) name the contact address, whether it has set up .oss-scanner/ in its repository, and
# whether projects/<name>/ follows the rules. The comment informs the review and decides nothing. A pull request
# that touches nothing under projects/ gets no comment.
#
# pull_request_target, not pull_request: a pull request from a fork gets a read-only token, which cannot comment.
# That makes this workflow run with the base repository's token on input from anyone, so it is split in two:
#   gather   reads the pull request through the GitHub API, as data, with a read-only token. Its checkout is the base
#            branch (the default for pull_request_target), never the pull request, so no code from the pull request runs.
#   comment  holds the only write permission, and does nothing but post the text gather produced.
# Values from the event reach the scripts through environment variables, never by ${{ }} substitution into them.
#
# A pull request that has had none of the events below since this workflow was added has no comment. Someone with
# write access can ask for one, or for a fresh one, from the same two jobs with the same permissions:
#   gh workflow run triage.yaml -f pr=123
# That run checks out the branch it is started on (main, unless --ref names another): still never a pull request.
# For many pull requests, leave a few minutes between runs. A run makes up to 30 API requests, every run in this
# repository draws on the same 1,000 an hour, and a check that finds them spent says "could not be checked".

# A run started by hand is listed under the number it was given, as a pull request's is under its title.
run-name: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title || format('Pull request {0}', inputs.pr) }}

on:
  pull_request_target:
    # edited: the comment reports on the checklist in the description.
    types: [opened, edited, reopened, synchronize]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      pr:
        description: "Number of the pull request to comment on"
        required: true
        type: number

permissions: {}

concurrency:
  group: triage-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || inputs.pr }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  gather:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: read
    outputs:
      comment: ${{ steps.triage.outputs.comment }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1 (sha-pinned)
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Write the comment
        id: triage
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number || inputs.pr }}
        run: |
          python3 -c 'import yaml' 2>/dev/null || { sudo apt-get update -qq && sudo apt-get install -y -qq python3-yaml; }
          # A random delimiter, so that no text in the comment can end the output early.
          delimiter="triage-$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
          {
            echo "comment<<$delimiter"
            python3 .github/scripts/triage.py --repo "$REPO" --pr "$PR"
            echo "$delimiter"
          } >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  comment:
    needs: gather
    if: needs.gather.outputs.comment != ''
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 2
    permissions:
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - name: Post the comment, or update the one already there
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number || inputs.pr }}
          COMMENT: ${{ needs.gather.outputs.comment }}
        run: |
          # The CLA workflow also comments as github-actions[bot]; ours is the one that starts with the marker.
          existing=$(gh api "repos/$REPO/issues/$PR/comments" --paginate \
            --jq '.[] | select(.user.login == "github-actions[bot]" and (.body | startswith("<!-- oss-scanner-triage -->"))) | .id')
          existing=${existing%%$'\n'*}
          if [ -n "$existing" ]; then
            jq -n --arg body "$COMMENT" '{body: $body}' | gh api --method PATCH "repos/$REPO/issues/comments/$existing" --input - > /dev/null
          else
            jq -n --arg body "$COMMENT" '{body: $body}' | gh api --method POST "repos/$REPO/issues/$PR/comments" --input - > /dev/null
          fi
